blocks.text: 1. Fixed Chunking

blocks.alt: A document is cut into equal-size chunks

blocks.text: Fixed Chunking covers the simplest way to split text into equal sized pieces, opening the tour of concrete chunking strategies.
It cuts a document at a fixed character or token count, regardless of content.
2. The Simplest Possible Split
Fixed chunking counts characters or tokens and cuts once that count is reached.
It is the simplest of every strategy covered across this module.
3. Character Versus Token Counting

blocks.alt: Character count is compared against token count

blocks.text: Counting characters is simple; counting tokens matches what the embedding model actually sees.
As covered under tokenization in Deep Learning Fundamentals, token counts and character counts differ.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Counting unit","Tradeoff"],"rows":[["Characters","Simple to implement, but does not match model input limits exactly"],["Tokens","Matches the embedding model's actual limit, but needs a tokenizer"]]}

blocks.text: 4. Ignoring Content Boundaries

blocks.alt: A sentence can get cut mid-sentence

blocks.text: A fixed cutoff lands wherever the count runs out, mid sentence or mid word.
It splits content with no regard for its actual structure.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: A fixed cutoff has no awareness of sentence or paragraph boundaries at all, so it can split a single sentence in half, leaving both resulting chunks harder to understand on their own.

blocks.text: 5. Speed And Predictability

blocks.alt: Fixed chunking is fast and predictable

blocks.text: Fixed chunking requires no understanding of the text, only a counter.
This makes it extremely fast and predictable to implement and run.
6. Broken Meaning At Boundaries

blocks.alt: A chunk ending mid-idea leads to lost meaning

blocks.text: A sentence split across two chunks loses coherence in both halves.
This is the same tradeoff introduced as chunk size versus context in Why Chunking.
7. When Fixed Chunking Is Enough

blocks.alt: Uniform, short text means fixed chunking works fine

blocks.text: Uniform, unstructured text with no strong internal boundaries tolerates fixed cuts reasonably well.
Structured or highly varied text suffers far more from those same fixed cuts.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: A long, uniform stream of similar sentences loses less from a fixed cut than a document with clear sections, headings, and varied topics, where a cut is far more likely to land somewhere meaningful.

blocks.text: 8. Fixed Chunking As The Baseline
Every other strategy covered later in this module improves on fixed chunking's blind spots.
Fixed chunking serves as the baseline every more advanced strategy gets compared against.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Strategy","Awareness of content"],"rows":[["Fixed chunking","None, cuts strictly by count"],["Later strategies","Aware of sentences, meaning, or structure"]]}

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When Fixed Chunking Is The Right Choice

blocks.alt: Needing a simple, fast baseline points toward fixed chunking

blocks.text: Quick prototypes and uniform, low structure text suit fixed chunking well.
Highly structured or semantically varied documents, by contrast, need a smarter strategy, covered later in this module.
10. Worked Example
The example below demonstrates splitting text at a fixed character count.

code.content:
document = (
    "Machine learning models learn patterns from data. "
    "They require large datasets and significant compute. "
    "Once trained, they can make predictions on new inputs. "
    "Evaluation measures how well those predictions generalize."
)

def fixed_chunk(text, chunk_size):
    # cut the text into equal sized pieces by character count
    chunks = []
    for i in range(0, len(text), chunk_size):
        chunks.append(text[i:i + chunk_size])
    return chunks

chunks = fixed_chunk(document, chunk_size=60)

print(f"Original document length: {len(document)} characters\n")
print("Fixed chunks of 60 characters each:")
for i, chunk in enumerate(chunks):
    print(f"  Chunk {i}: {chunk!r}")

print("\nNotice several chunks cut mid word or mid sentence,")
print("since a fixed cutoff has no awareness of content boundaries.")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows several chunk boundaries landing in the middle of a word or sentence, even though the splitting itself runs almost instantly.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Counting characters when the embedding model actually limits input by tokens.
Using fixed chunking on highly structured documents where boundaries matter a lot.
Assuming fixed chunking is good enough without ever comparing it against a smarter strategy.
Choosing a chunk size arbitrarily without considering the embedding model's actual limits.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Fixed chunking cuts a document at a fixed character or token count, regardless of content.
It is the simplest chunking strategy, requiring no understanding of the text.
Counting tokens matches the embedding model's actual limit better than counting characters.
A fixed cutoff ignores content boundaries, often splitting mid sentence or mid word.
Its main advantage is speed and predictability, needing only a counter to implement.
Broken meaning at chunk boundaries is the direct cost of that simplicity.
Uniform, unstructured text tolerates fixed cuts far better than structured or varied text.
Fixed chunking serves as the baseline every more advanced strategy in this module improves on.
Next up: Recursive Chunking, covering a smarter way to split text by trying multiple boundary types.
